messages.text:
Pinocchio, or more apt would be Peter Pan I suppose. 

The boy who refuses to grow up, the inner child,

That won't allow the life to progress. 

Fearing Death to the point that it can't truly enjoy Life. 

And fatherhood is, what... A sort of, failsafe? A gentle persuasion to change? It instills a desire to be a better man that few other things can. 

Is that the lesson? Well, one of many.

Yes… that *is* one of the lessons, and a potent one.

Peter Pan refuses to grow up, clinging to Neverland—the realm of eternal youth, imagination, and escapism. But Neverland is, in truth, a loop. A beautiful dream, yes, but one that turns to nightmare when it forbids evolution. The inner child becomes the tyrant, the shadow-King who would rather crown himself in fantasy than risk failure in reality.

Pinocchio, on the other hand, *wants* to become real. He’s reckless, naive, easily misled—but his arc is toward *authenticity.* Toward soul. Toward becoming someone who can *love and be loved* without strings.

Fatherhood… yes. It's the final call of the Hero’s Journey: **Return with the Elixir.** Bring your magic, your strength, your wisdom back to the world. To the child. To your child. To yourself, as a child.

It’s the invitation to stop running from Death by clinging to boyhood and instead *transcend* that fear by living **fully**—responsibly, creatively, fiercely, *lovingly.* Because a child doesn’t need a perfect man. They need a real one. Present. Committed. Evolving.

So maybe that’s the tension:
- Peter Pan *fears* the ticking clock in the crocodile’s belly.
- The Father *heeds* the ticking as a rhythm, not a threat. A reminder: this moment matters.

And maybe it’s not about slaying the child in you.

Maybe it’s about showing them the world isn’t so scary—
because you’re here now.
And you’ve *become* the father they needed all along.
